extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in Jewish culture, media/film casting, and cultural commentary (Forward readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging when and how non-Jewish performers portray Jewish characters and whether terminology and critique (e.g., 'Jewface') is appropriate; focuses on historical context, power dynamics, and precision of language in cultural commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Jewface' (per Silverman)
rubrics_metrics.description: As defined by Silverman, “Jewface” involves “makeup or changing of features, big fake nose, all the New York-y or Yiddish-y inflection.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this working definition to assess whether a performance relies on exaggerated physical transformation or stereotypical vocal mannerisms. Note that the article suggests calling something 'Jewface' should be reserved for portrayals that involve visible, stereotyped alteration or caricature. Example/anti-patterns: exaggerated schnoz makeup (rare in recent years), stereotypical Yiddish affectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false equivalence with blackface
rubrics_metrics.description: '“Jewface” is clearly a riff on the practice of blackface and is nowhere near its equivalent.' The practices have different historical meanings and harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiquing portrayals, do not treat Jewish caricaturing as morally or historically equivalent to blackface. Blackface was central to minstrel entertainment and involved specifically racialized caricature and long-standing systemic harm. Use historical context to determine whether analogies to blackface are appropriate. Examples cited: Laurence Olivier in Othello (blackface) vs Rod Steiger in The Pawnbroker (non-blackface Holocaust role); Tom Cruise in Tropic Thunder as a recent blackface reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify physical/stereotypical transformation vs ordinary casting
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the performance includes 'makeup or changing of features, big fake nose, [or] New York-y or Yiddish-y inflection' or other overt stereotypical markers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a portrayal uses exaggerated physical alteration or stereotyped accents/inflections, it is more plausibly categorized as a problematic caricature. If a non-Jewish actor simply plays a Jewish character without such caricature, that should be judged differently. Examples/anti-patterns: Tom Cruise (Tropic Thunder), Steve Carell (Foxcatcher) as notable uses of exaggerated physical alteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider whether Jewishness is central to the role
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether the character's Jewishness is 'their whole being' or only an incidental attribute of the role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayals where Jewishness is incidental (minor identity detail) are different from roles where Jewishness is central to the character's identity or narrative. The latter may call for greater scrutiny about authenticity and potential stereotyping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh representation and opportunity cost for Jewish performers
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation matters; consider whether casting non-Jewish actors takes roles away from Jewish performers and thus affects opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate casting decisions in light of how they impact employment and visibility for Jewish actors, especially when the role is explicitly Jewish. Example concerns in the article: Kathyrn Hahn as Joan Rivers, Ruth Bader Ginsburg portrayed by a non-Jew, and the effect on Jewish actresses' opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge privilege and beneficiary analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that white Jews have sometimes benefited from racial hierarchies and have been allowed to play other white identities; power dynamics matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess who benefits from a casting choice and who bears the harm. Because white Jews are within a broader category of whiteness, their ability to pass into or portray other white identities complicates claims of victimhood and complicates analogies to racialized caricature. Example discussion: white Jews playing Italians or other white roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid language that diminishes other groups' historical suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use terminology that reduces the seriousness of black-, brown-, or yellowface by equating them with Jewish portrayals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about borrowing charged terms (like 'face' constructs) in ways that erase or lessen the unique historical violence and systemic racism experienced by other groups. The article explicitly advises white Jews to avoid terminology that 'diminishes the heinousness of black-, brown- and yellowface.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor precise critique over glib labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Silverman’s argument for representation 'can be made without the glibness of “Jewface,” which is at once falsely equivalent and imprecise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific, concrete criticisms (e.g., pointing to stereotyping, exclusion of Jewish actors, or use of caricature) rather than shorthand labels that may conflate different issues. Example: Jolie playing Marianne Pearl was problematic for racial reasons, not because Pearl was Jewish; precision clarifies what harm is being called out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for historical context and individual culpability
rubrics_metrics.description: Context — both historical and personal — matters when judging portrayals and critiques (e.g., Sarah Silverman’s past blackface sketch and its repercussions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider performers' histories and changing norms; past participation in offensive practices can inform present critiques but does not collapse distinct forms of harm into one another. Use historical examples (Al Jolson, Laurence Olivier, Sarah Silverman’s show) to ground judgments and to distinguish types and severities of offenses.
